chapter: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
title: No longer playing; left his horn in Detroit
summary: He has not played since January 1970, lost his horn behind his cousin's settee, and dislikes rock and commercial music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: So, you have not been actively playing music since 1970?
No, 1970 -- yeah, I think it was January the 7th. I don't even have a horn now.
You don't have a horn? What happened to your horn?
I left it in Detroit behind my cousin's settee.
My cousin, I don't think, has pawned it yet.
Oh, I don't think I need it any more. I don't think I want it anymore. I've lost all feeling for music.
-- about five weeks ago when we started talking, you were talking about wanting to play.

No. No, not the way -- it's all right to pick up your horn around the house, but music has a different -- has a different thing today than it used to be. It used to be a development of your inner feelings. I mean you played what you felt, but today it's strictly a commercial aspect. Some of this music that they have -- I could never fit in because it has no expression of inner feelings.
You're talking about the contemporary rock oriented music?

Yeah, I don't -- well, there's many of us that just don't seem to be able to fit in it from a whole lot of -- well, from several angles of it. I can't see the looks of them. I can't see the antics of them. I can't see the music they play, or if you call it music. And so, it's time to get out. That's all.
But there are many people playing music other than rock.

Not to the great degree. They're gradually coming around, but -- and they will finally, I'm quite sure, come back to a good melody and good music as I call it. But this is a mad age right now, and I can't fit in it, so I better stay out of it.
